subject: Endocrine
subtopic: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
vignette: A 22-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and rapid deep breathing after missing insulin injections for 2 days while fighting a respiratory infection. Laboratory studies show glucose 480 mg/dL, pH 7.18, bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, anion gap 22, and large urine ketones.
question: Which of the following best explains the accumulation of ketone bodies in this patient?

options.text: Increased insulin driving glucose uptake and suppressing lipolysis
Reduced glucagon activity with increased hepatic glycogen storage
Oxidation of glucose through glycolysis generating acetyl-CoA from pyruvate
Insulin deficiency with lipolysis and free fatty acid oxidation producing beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate
Decreased counter-regulatory hormones with enhanced peripheral glucose utilization

explanation_correct: Insulin deficiency, here triggered by noncompliance and increased requirements from infection, removes the normal inhibition of lipolysis in adipose tissue. Released free fatty acids are oxidized by the liver into ketone bodies, predominantly beta-hydroxybutyrate greater than acetoacetate. The result is the high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with ketonuria that defines DKA. Insulin is deficient and ketones are present, the opposite of HHS.

explanation_incorrect.A: Insulin is deficient rather than increased in DKA; insulin would suppress lipolysis and ketogenesis, which is the opposite of this patient's state.
explanation_incorrect.B: Glucagon and other counter-regulatory hormones are relatively elevated in DKA and promote ketogenesis; glycogen storage is not the source of ketone bodies.
explanation_incorrect.C: In insulin deficiency, tissues cannot effectively use glucose; ketone bodies arise from free fatty acid oxidation in the liver, not from glucose oxidation through glycolysis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Counter-regulatory hormones are increased, not decreased, in DKA, and peripheral glucose utilization falls because insulin is lacking.

educationalObjective: DKA results from insulin deficiency with increased lipolysis and free fatty acid oxidation, producing beta-hydroxybutyrate greater than acetoacetate and a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

subject: Endocrine
subtopic: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
vignette: A 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus arrives with hyperglycemia, a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, and large urine ketones. She is tachypneic with deep, labored breathing, and her breath has a fruity odor.
question: The deep, rapid breathing in this patient is best explained by which of the following?

options.text: A primary respiratory alkalosis from anxiety-induced hyperventilation
Respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis through carbon dioxide removal
Central neurogenic hyperventilation caused by cerebral edema
Hypoxemia from pulmonary edema triggering reflex tachypnea
Sepsis-induced acute respiratory distress syndrome

explanation_correct: Kussmaul respirations are the deep, rapid breathing that compensates for a metabolic acidosis: the patient hyperventilates to lower the arterial PCO2 and partially normalize pH. This is one element of the 'DKA is Deadly' mnemonic, along with delirium/psychosis, abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting, dehydration, and fruity breath from exhaled acetone. The breathing is a normal physiologic response to the low bicarbonate, not a primary lung disorder.

explanation_incorrect.A: Anxiety can cause hyperventilation, but a primary respiratory alkalosis would show a high pH and low PCO2; this patient's deep breathing compensates for a low bicarbonate and low pH.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cerebral edema is a serious DKA complication that produces altered mental status, not the compensatory deep breathing pattern driven by acidosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hypoxemia from pulmonary edema would cause dyspnea and low oxygen saturation, not the characteristic compensatory hyperventilation of metabolic acidosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Acute respiratory distress syndrome from sepsis is a primary lung injury and is not the mechanism of Kussmaul respirations in an anion-gap acidosis.

educationalObjective: Kussmaul respirations in DKA are respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis, not a primary pulmonary process.

subject: Endocrine
subtopic: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
vignette: A 24-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus in DKA has a serum potassium of 5.2 mEq/L and peaked T waves on ECG. He has had vomiting and polyuria for 2 days. Despite the elevated serum potassium, his clinicians include potassium replacement in his treatment plan.
question: Which of the following best explains why total body potassium is depleted despite this elevated serum potassium?

options.text: Insulin deficiency and acidosis shift potassium out of cells while osmotic diuresis drives urinary potassium loss
Aldosterone deficiency causes renal potassium wasting and lowers serum potassium
Excess potassium intake expands the extracellular pool without changing intracellular stores
Vomiting causes direct potassium loss that raises serum potassium through hemoconcentration
Acidosis drives potassium into cells, lowering serum potassium while total body stores stay normal

explanation_correct: In DKA, low insulin and acidosis shift potassium out of cells in exchange for hydrogen ions, so serum potassium can be normal or elevated even though intracellular and total body potassium are depleted. At the same time, osmotic diuresis causes substantial urinary potassium loss, further depleting total body stores. Insulin therapy drives potassium back into cells and can unmask severe hypokalemia, which is why potassium is replaced as part of treatment.

explanation_incorrect.B: Aldosterone is not deficient; volume depletion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. The dominant mechanisms here are the transcellular shift from low insulin/acidosis and urinary loss from osmotic diuresis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Excess potassium intake would increase total body potassium rather than deplete it; this patient's problem is potassium loss, not gain.
explanation_incorrect.D: Vomiting does cause potassium loss but would not raise serum potassium, and hemoconcentration does not account for the intracellular depletion described.
explanation_incorrect.E: Acidosis shifts potassium out of cells, not into them; serum potassium is normal or elevated in DKA, not low, and total body stores are reduced.

educationalObjective: In DKA, normal or high serum potassium masks intracellular and total body potassium depletion caused by transcellular shift and osmotic diuresis.

subject: Endocrine
subtopic: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
vignette: A 78-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is brought in with severe dehydration, lethargy, and focal neurologic deficits after several days of polyuria and limited ability to drink. Laboratory studies show glucose 720 mg/dL, serum osmolality 335 mOsm/kg, pH 7.42, bicarbonate 25 mEq/L, and no urine or blood ketones.
question: Which of the following findings best distinguishes this hyperglycemic emergency from diabetic ketoacidosis?

options.text: Profound hyperglycemia with increased serum osmolality
Dehydration with signs of volume depletion
Lethargy and altered mental status
Advanced age and type 2 diabetes mellitus
Absence of ketosis with a normal pH

explanation_correct: This is hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state: profound hyperglycemia drives osmotic diuresis, dehydration, and a high serum osmolality, but enough insulin is present to suppress lipolysis so ketones are deficient and pH is normal. The absence of significant ketosis and acidosis is the key laboratory distinction from DKA, in which ketones are present and a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis is expected.

explanation_incorrect.A: Profound hyperglycemia occurs in both DKA and HHS; although osmolality is typically higher in HHS, hyperglycemia alone does not distinguish the two emergencies.
explanation_incorrect.B: Dehydration from osmotic diuresis is a feature of both disorders, so it cannot discriminate between them.
explanation_incorrect.C: Altered mental status occurs in both: delirium or psychosis is seen in DKA, while lethargy and focal deficits are common in HHS.
explanation_incorrect.D: Advanced age and type 2 diabetes are the classic demographic context for HHS but are risk factors rather than a definitive distinguishing laboratory finding.

educationalObjective: HHS is distinguished from DKA by profound hyperglycemia and high osmolality with minimal ketosis and a normal pH, reflecting preserved insulin activity.

subject: Endocrine
subtopic: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
vignette: An 82-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus becomes confused after a week of illness with poor oral intake. Laboratory studies show glucose 810 mg/dL, serum osmolality 340 mOsm/kg, pH 7.41, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, and negative ketones. His serum potassium is 4.8 mEq/L.
question: Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of this patient's condition?

options.text: Absolute insulin deficiency causing unrestrained lipolysis and ketogenesis
Insulin excess driving glucose into cells and producing hypoglycemia
Profound hyperglycemia causing osmotic diuresis with dehydration and elevated serum osmolality, with enough insulin to suppress ketogenesis
Primary renal failure causing an inability to excrete glucose and water
Cortisol excess with secondary aldosterone deficiency as the primary driver

explanation_correct: In HHS, profound hyperglycemia exceeds the renal threshold and causes an excessive osmotic diuresis, leading to dehydration and a marked rise in serum osmolality. Classically this occurs in older patients with type 2 diabetes and a limited ability to drink, such as during illness. Residual insulin secretion is sufficient to inhibit lipolysis and ketogenesis, so ketones are deficient and pH is normal; intracellular potassium is reduced despite a normal or elevated serum potassium.

explanation_incorrect.A: Absolute insulin deficiency with unrestrained ketogenesis describes DKA, not HHS; in HHS the remaining insulin suppresses ketone production.
explanation_incorrect.B: Insulin excess would lower glucose and cause hypoglycemia, the opposite of the profound hyperglycemia observed here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Primary renal failure is not the mechanism; the osmotic diuresis results from hyperglycemia itself, even with initially normal renal function.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cortisol excess and aldosterone deficiency are not the driver of HHS; the core mechanism is hyperglycemia-induced osmotic diuresis with preserved insulin.

educationalObjective: HHS arises from profound hyperglycemia and osmotic diuresis in older type 2 diabetics, with residual insulin preventing significant ketosis.

subject: Endocrine
subtopic: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
vignette: A 30-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus is treated for DKA with intravenous fluids and an intravenous insulin infusion. Her glucose falls to 250 mg/dL, but her bicarbonate and anion gap have not fully normalized and ketones remain elevated.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to avoid a complication of therapy?

options.text: Stop the insulin infusion immediately because the glucose has improved
Add dextrose-containing fluids while continuing insulin until the ketoacidosis resolves
Administer intravenous bicarbonate to rapidly correct the acidosis
Give an oral sulfonylurea to stimulate endogenous insulin secretion
Discontinue potassium replacement because serum potassium has normalized

explanation_correct: Treatment of DKA and HHS is intravenous fluids, intravenous insulin, and potassium repletion. Because insulin lowers glucose faster than it clears ketones, dextrose is added once glucose falls into the 250 to 300 mg/dL range so that insulin can be continued until the ketoacidosis and anion gap fully resolve. Stopping insulin early would leave the ketosis untreated, while continuing insulin without glucose risks hypoglycemia.

explanation_incorrect.A: Stopping insulin when glucose improves would halt resolution of the ketosis and anion gap, which lag behind the glucose; insulin must be continued.
explanation_incorrect.C: Bicarbonate is not routinely indicated in DKA and can worsen intracellular acidosis and hypokalemia; the mainstay is fluids, insulin, and potassium.
explanation_incorrect.D: Sulfonylureas are not used in DKA management, and a patient with type 1 diabetes has no functioning beta cells to stimulate.
explanation_incorrect.E: Potassium replacement should continue to replete depleted intracellular stores even after serum potassium normalizes.

educationalObjective: In DKA, dextrose is added as glucose falls so intravenous insulin can be continued until ketosis resolves, while fluids and potassium repletion continue.
